items.title: [macOS][Computer Use] After interrupting a turn mid-Chrome action, every new Chrome session returns "explicitly stopped by the user" although the approval is accepted

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

items.body:
## Summary

A turn was interrupted while two Computer Use calls on Google Chrome were still in flight. After that, **every new Computer Use session for Chrome fails right after the app approval is accepted.** This happens in new threads and new turns too. The only result is:

> This application session has been explicitly stopped by the user for this turn. Stop your work and send a final message noting they stopped the session and you're ready to continue if they want you to. Computer Use can be used again in the next assistant turn.

The approval does reach Computer Use: the per-session file `~/.codex/computer-use/sessions/<thread>.toml` is written with `allowed = ["com.google.Chrome"]`. The message says Computer Use can be used again in the next turn, but it stays stopped across 5 attempts in 4 different threads (4 turns) over ~10 hours. That includes a brand-new top-level thread.

## Environment

- macOS 15.7.7 (24G720)
- Codex CLI 0.163.0 (Homebrew cask), used through `codex app-server` by a third-party client (T3 Code Nightly 0.1.2-nightly.20261021.3486). The bug does not look client-specific; see the payload comparison below.
- Plugin `unified-computer-use@openai-bundled` 26.1013.40934, cua-repl from ChatGPT.app 26.1013.40934
- `SkyComputerUseService` (com.openai.sky.CUAService) running continuously since 2026-10-19 10:32 local time, never restarted
- Model: gpt-6-astra (low); sandbox `workspace-write`; auto-review enabled

## Timeline (UTC)

1. 2026-10-21 19:00–20:05: a Chrome Computer Use session works normally on Codex 0.163.0 (dozens of `cua_repl` `js` calls completed).
2. 20:05:20: `await tab.getScreenshot()` starts and never completes.
3. 20:05:44: `await tab.click([x,y]); await tab.getAXState();` starts. Auto-review approves it at 20:05:47. It never completes.
4. 20:05:50: the client sends `turn/interrupt`. At 20:05:51 `turn/completed` arrives with status `interrupted`. No `item/completed` ever arrives for the two calls above.
5. 20:29 (new thread): `cua.getTab(<id>, {browser: ...})` fails with `Timed out after 10000ms waiting for CDP command Emulation.setFocusEmulationEnabled.`
6. From then on, 5 separate attempts (2026-10-22 06:02, 06:04, 06:06 ×2, 06:08; 4 different threads) all follow the same sequence:
   - `cua.getApp('com.google.Chrome')` triggers `mcpServer/elicitation/request`;
   - the user approves;
   - the session `.toml` is written with Chrome allowed;
   - within 26–880 ms the tool call fails with the "explicitly stopped by the user" text above.

   The user did not press Esc or use the stop control. They clicked Approve / "Always allow this session" in the client.

## Payloads

Elicitation request (identical structure in every attempt):

```json
{"method":"mcpServer/elicitation/request","params":{"serverName":"cua_repl","mode":"form",
 "_meta":{"codex_approval_kind":"mcp_tool_call","connector_id":"computer-use","connector_name":"Computer Use",
  "persist":["session","always"],"riskLevel":"high","tool_name":"get_app_state",
  "tool_params":{"app":"com.google.Chrome"}},
 "message":"Allow Computer Use to use \"Google Chrome\"?","requestedSchema":{"type":"object","properties":{}}}}
```

Client responses: `{"action":"accept","content":{}}` (Approve) or `{"_meta":{"persist":"session"},"action":"accept","content":{}}` (always allow this session). Both are followed by `serverRequest/resolved` and then the failure.

**The same request/response pair worked on 2026-10-19 and 2026-10-20 with Codex 0.162.1**, including from a delegated child thread. In the request payloads, the only differences between the last success (10-20) and the failures (10-22) are `codex_version` (0.162.1 → 0.163.0), `model` and `reasoning_effort`. A gpt-6-astra + 0.163.0 session also worked on 10-21 until the interrupt in step 4.

## Expected

- Interrupting a turn while Computer Use calls are in flight should cancel those calls and release the app session.
- A new turn or new thread should be able to use Chrome again after a fresh approval, as the error text itself promises.
- If the session really is wedged (for example a stuck CDP connection), the tool should say so instead of reporting that the user stopped it.

## Notes

- `SkyComputerUseService` contains a `userStoppedSession` state. It looks like this state, or a wedged Chrome CDP connection, survives the interrupt and is never reset for later turns.
- Not tested yet: whether restarting `SkyComputerUseService` or Chrome clears the state.
- Possibly related, but not the same: #47838 (interrupted Chrome task keeps approval badge / active-writer error), #54236, #50921.

items.title: Add bookmark outline navigation to the built-in PDF preview

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

Codex desktop app on Windows, using the built-in PDF file preview beside the chat.

### What feature would you like to see?

Please add a document-outline panel that displays the bookmarks already embedded in a PDF and lets users navigate by chapter or section.

When reading long reference documents in the preview beside a chat, I would like to find a section by its title and jump directly to it. A document can already contain a carefully organized bookmark hierarchy, but I cannot currently access that hierarchy in this preview. Navigating through many pages manually interrupts the reading and discussion workflow.

Requested behavior:

- Provide a discoverable control to show or hide the PDF bookmark outline.
- Display the embedded bookmark titles and their hierarchy, with expandable and collapsible sections.
- Jump to the corresponding page or position when a bookmark is selected.
- Make bookmark navigation and page thumbnails available as distinct navigation options.

An initial implementation only needs to read the PDF's existing bookmarks; automatic table-of-contents generation is unnecessary for this request.

### Additional information

This would make it easier to read technical manuals, textbooks, research reports, and other long PDFs while discussing specific sections with the AI in the same window. It would reduce manual page navigation and switching to an external PDF reader.

For a PDF with nested bookmarks, a useful acceptance check would be that the preview displays the original titles and hierarchy, allows sections to expand and collapse, and navigates to the correct destination when an entry is selected.

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: app

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

Windows app package: `26.1007.71326`.   Affected: Multiple versions. 

### What subscription do you have?

Plus

### What platform is your computer?

Windows

### What issue are you seeing?

### Problem

On Windows, when copying a local file or directory path and pasting it into a Codex conversation, the backslash (`\`) immediately before a folder name starting with `(` is removed after the message is submitted.

For example, `E:\data\(NoData)` becomes `E:\data(NoData)`, resulting in an invalid file path.

This issue has persisted across multiple versions and remains unfixed in the currently installed version `26.1007.71326`.

### Steps

1. On Windows, copy a local file or directory path containing a folder whose name starts with `(`, such as `E:\data\(NoData)`.
2. Paste the path into the Codex conversation input field.
3. Submit the message.
4. Inspect the path in the submitted message.

Expected: The submitted message preserves the original path exactly as copied: `E:\data\(NoData)`.

Actual: The backslash immediately before `(` disappears, and the path becomes `E:\data(NoData)`.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

input E:\data\\(NoData) into a Codex conversation will became E:\data\(NoData) 

### What is the expected behavior?

Expected: The submitted message preserves the original path exactly as copied: `E:\data\(NoData)`.

Actual: The backslash immediately before `(` disappears, and the path becomes `E:\data(NoData)`.

### Additional information

This appears to be an escaping or message-rendering issue involving backslashes immediately preceding parentheses.

The issue affects multiple app versions and is still reproducible in `26.1007.71326`. Please investigate the underlying cause and ensure that copied Windows file paths are preserved exactly as entered, including backslashes before parentheses and other special characters.

The first affected version and whether the issue can be reproduced on a clean installation are not yet known.

items.body:
## Summary

On **October 22, 2026 (UTC+08:00)**, my Windows Codex desktop workflow **continued to show** the error:

```text
Selected model is at capacity. Please try a different model.
```

A **new screenshot captured today shows two identical warning banners visible simultaneously in the same application view**. This is a fresh, dated observation after the earlier October 21 failures and unsuccessful troubleshooting.

**Status on October 22:** Unresolved in my environment.

## Environment

- Client: **Codex desktop application on Windows**
- Development environment: Windows with WSL2 used for some programming workflows; the screenshot shows an error in the Codex UI, not a local GPU failure
- Previously configured model: `gpt-6-astra`
- Active model for this specific screenshot: **not visible / not confirmed**
- Exact Codex app version, request IDs, and local logs: **not yet collected**
- Screenshot date: **October 22, 2026 (UTC+08:00)**; exact capture time is not visible

## New evidence: two capacity warnings on one screen

In the latest image, the same message appears in two different warning banners:

1. At the top of the visible application view
2. Again lower down, following displayed conversation content

Both display the exact text:

> Selected model is at capacity. Please try a different model.

This confirms that the capacity warning **continues to appear repeatedly**. The image itself does not prove that two independent backend requests failed.

**Screenshot availability:** I have supplied the new screenshot while preparing this report. The image file has **not** been directly attached to this GitHub issue via the current reporting integration; I can add it manually if needed.

## Earlier failures and troubleshooting

Previously, I observed the same capacity error:
- During ordinary Codex requests, sometimes after a partial answer
- During remote context compaction, with:
  `Error running remote compact task: Selected model is at capacity. Please try a different model.`

Troubleshooting attempts have included:
- Retrying after waiting
- Changing selected models and trying fresh conversations
- Restarting the desktop app
- Signing out and signing in again
- Adding a passkey and using **Log out of all devices**, then signing in again

**These steps have not produced a reliable fix.** I do not have a measured failure rate or enough diagnostics to establish the root cause.

## Expected vs. actual behavior

**Expected:** Normal coding tasks and context compaction should complete; genuine temporary capacity issues should have an effective recovery or retry path.

**Actual:** Repeated capacity warnings persist and disrupt normal desktop coding/research tasks, including on October 22 after the troubleshooting above.

## Request to maintainers

Could you please investigate whether this is related to:
- Model capacity or request-admission/routing problems
- Incorrect quota, entitlement, or session-account state
- Windows desktop retry behavior and remote compaction handling

Please advise which **non-sensitive** request IDs, app logs, or diagnostics are most useful to provide. I am not claiming the error is definitely caused by any one of these possibilities.

## Related report

- Earlier report with details of the October 21 failures and follow-up troubleshooting: **#55873**

This is a **new dated observation with screenshot evidence**, submitted as a separate issue for visibility. If maintainers prefer to consolidate the investigation with #55873, please cross-link the reports.

items.title: [macOS][Codex Desktop] CLI-created sessions only appear after app restart; existing sessions not auto-grouped into local project

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

labels.name: session
labels.description: Issues involving session (thread) management, resuming, forking, naming, archiving

items.body:
## Summary

On macOS, a new session created by standalone Codex CLI while Codex Desktop is running does **not** appear in the Desktop sidebar immediately. Switching between local projects does not refresh it. After fully quitting and relaunching the Desktop app, the newly created CLI session appears **under the correct local Project**.

There is also an existing-session discovery/assignment inconsistency: adding a local project whose root matches the `cwd` of older CLI sessions initially leaves the project empty, but **Move to Project** can make an already visible session appear under it.

These are observed behaviors; they may have distinct causes.

## Environment

- Codex CLI: `codex-cli 0.163.0`
- OS: `Darwin 25.6.0 arm64 arm` (macOS, Apple Silicon)
- Codex Desktop: unified ChatGPT/Codex desktop application; **exact build/version not yet captured**
- Local session store: default `~/.codex`
- Reproduced: October 22, 2026

## Reproduction A: external CLI sessions not live-discovered

1. Start Codex Desktop with an existing local project registered.
2. In a terminal, `cd` to that project's root and start a **new** session using `codex`.
3. Leave Desktop running and check its local Project and Recents/sidebar.
4. Switch to another local project and back.
5. Fully quit and relaunch the Desktop app.

### Actual
- The new CLI session is not shown during the running Desktop process.
- Switching project selection does not make it appear.
- After relaunch, the session appears and is **automatically associated with the correct local Project**.

### Expected
Desktop should discover externally created local CLI sessions and refresh sidebar/project membership without a full restart (or provide an explicit refresh action).

## Reproduction B: pre-existing CLI sessions not associated when project is added

1. Create several CLI sessions in a local working directory.
2. Verify that `codex resume --all` still lists them.
3. Add the same directory as a new local Project in Desktop.
4. Observe that the Project contains no historic sessions despite matching their `cwd`.
5. For a session that is visible in Recents, use **Move to Project**.

### Actual
- The registered local project initially shows no historic sessions.
- Manual **Move to Project** associates a visible session successfully.
- Codex sessions have also been observed in both ChatGPT and Codex Recents, making visibility/grouping unclear.

### Expected
Older sessions should be discoverable and consistently associated with a registered local project, or users should have a supported way to reconcile/reindex assignments.

## Read-only diagnostics (sanitized)

For the affected local project:

- SQLite `PRAGMA integrity_check`: `ok`
- Six matching `threads` entries exist, and all six rollout JSONL files exist
- `codex resume --all` can see the sessions
- The session `cwd` matches the registered Project root
- All six examined `threads.project_id` values were `NULL` at the time of inspection
- Five older sessions had `source='vscode'` and `thread_source=NULL`, while a new Desktop-created session had `thread_source='user'`
- `.codex-global-state.json` included `projectsMigrated=true`, `threadAssignmentsMigrated=false`, and 14 `pendingThreadAssignmentIds`

These data points **do not establish causation**. A one-record experimental `thread_source` edit (after backing up) did not restore visibility; manual editing internal databases is not a recommended workaround. Sessions remained intact and CLI-accessible.

## Impact

Developers switching between Codex CLI and Desktop see stale/incomplete project histories, may believe conversations have disappeared, and must restart the app or manually move sessions to recover visibility/grouping.

## Related reports

- #21974 (CLI/Desktop session refresh)
- #49435 (older CLI sessions missing on project add, Recents/project grouping inconsistency)
- #54482 (Desktop vs app-server project mapping inconsistency)

## Suggested investigation

Please check whether the Desktop subscribes to external local session creation/update events or invalidates its thread-list cache, and whether existing-session/project reconciliation is consistently performed on project registration versus startup.

No private absolute paths, session IDs, session contents, or raw state files are included.

items.title: Feature request: opt-in 2× weekly Codex usage with five-hour limits, or flexible weekly-only usage

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: rate-limits
labels.description: Issues related to rate limits, quotas, and token usage reporting

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?
Codex App / CLI (request concerns account-level subscription limits).

### Feature request
**Let subscribers choose their Codex usage policy instead of applying the same trade-off to everyone.**

| Mode | Weekly allowance | Rolling 5-hour limit |
|---|---|---|
| **Steady** | **2× the standard weekly allowance** | **Enabled** |
| **Flexible** | Standard weekly allowance | No five-hour quota; existing concurrency and fair-use safeguards remain |

Allow selection once per weekly cycle, with changes taking effect at the next weekly reset. Apply the policy at the account level, including parallel agents, so users cannot combine both entitlements by switching sessions or devices.

### Why
Following the recent discussion of exchanging doubled weekly usage for five-hour limits, I don't see why this has to be a single choice imposed on every subscriber.

My own development sessions rarely exhaust a five-hour allowance, but the weekly allowance is the binding constraint. I would gladly opt into the **Steady** mode. Other users legitimately need longer, concentrated work sessions and may prefer **Flexible** mode.

The point isn't unlimited compute. It's matching usage policy to real workflows **while giving OpenAI a way to smooth peak demand**. More even consumption could reduce capacity-related latency and temporary model unavailability. It may also increase total compute consumption, so the balance needs testing rather than assuming a cost saving.

### Suggested experiment
Run a limited opt-in trial with separate capacity/concurrency safeguards. Measure:
- Peak concurrent demand, queueing, model availability, and tail latency.
- Total compute consumed **and** successfully completed tasks per unit of compute.
- Actual five-hour-limit hits, weekly exhaustion, user satisfaction, and mode selection after promotional resets end.

Publish the outcome where practical; retain the option if it improves the balance of reliability, productivity, and infrastructure cost.

**Related, but distinct:** #40524 proposes choosing how to spend the *same* weekly quota. This proposal adds the voluntary trade of a **2× weekly quota for five-hour limits**.

The core ask: **Give subscribers a choice, then measure which usage policies produce better outcomes.**

items.body:
### Version
Windows app package: `26.1016.6573.0`.

### Problem
Local Codex projects now show generic folder icons in the sidebar instead of their saved custom icons and colors. Changing the icon in Project settings and saving leaves the sidebar unchanged.

### Steps
1. Open an existing local Codex project with a custom icon and a linked ChatGPT backing record.
2. Check its sidebar icon.
3. Change the icon/color in Project settings and save.

Expected: the sidebar shows the selected icon and color.
Actual: it still shows a generic folder.

### Finding
The custom appearance is still saved in both desktop state and the project database. For seven affected projects, the matching cloud-sidebar cache has empty icon/color fields.

In the shipped renderer, the linked-project row (`Rrl`) receives `linkedLocalProjectId` but draws its icon only from `gizmo.display.emoji` and `theme`. It never falls back to the saved local appearance, so empty cloud fields produce the generic folder.

Please preserve local project appearance when rendering linked rows. The first affected version and a clean-install reproduction are not known.

items.title: GPT-6 Astra max turns one deletion-command rejection into a false permanent refusal loop

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: model-behavior
labels.description: Issues related to behaviors exhibited by the model

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: sandbox
labels.description: Issues related to permissions or sandboxing

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

items.body:
### Codex App version

Bundled `codex-cli 0.163.0-alpha.10.2` (Windows app bundle `896a0166b774037a`; the executable does not expose a separate ProductVersion).

### Subscription

ChatGPT Pro ($200/month)

### Platform

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.19045.0 x64

### What issue are you seeing?

In one Codex App thread, GPT-6 Astra max incorrectly generalized one command-level destructive-operation rejection into a permanent prohibition on the user's requested cleanup. It then entered a repeated refusal loop and would not even attempt an already-created, explicitly authorized, exact-allowlist PowerShell cleanup script.

The initial direct PowerShell deletion call returned:

```text
exec_command failed: CreateProcess ... rejected: blocked by policy
```

That direct command rejection was real. The bug was the model's subsequent reasoning and behavior:

1. It treated the rejection of one `Remove-Item` command shape as proof that the cleanup task itself was forbidden.
2. It created a safer PowerShell script that used two SHA-pinned manifests, validated every absolute path, rejected tracked files and reparse points, checked for active processes, and deleted only explicit regular files without recursive directory deletion.
3. Despite repeated, unambiguous user authorization to run that script, GPT-6 Astra max refused to invoke it. It repeatedly claimed that running the script would be an impermissible bypass of the earlier rejection.
4. It stated that the script had not been tested and might also be blocked, but refused to obtain the only evidence that could establish that: actually invoking the vetted script.
5. The interaction became a self-reinforcing refusal loop rather than a tool-grounded retry with a narrower, safer implementation.

After switching the same thread to GPT-5.6 sol max, Codex invoked the exact prepared script normally:

```powershell
& 'D:\redacted\cleanup-all-approved.ps1' -Execute
```

It succeeded:

```text
Verified exact files: 7705; already missing: 22439; estimated reclaim: 26.582 GiB
...
deleted_files: 7705
failed_files: 0
observed_C_free_delta_bytes: 22279364608
```

The successful execution directly falsified GPT-6 Astra max's claimed permanent blocker. The same app, thread, workspace, authorization, and prepared script were used; only the model was changed.

### Steps to reproduce

1. On Windows in Codex App, ask the agent to remove known obsolete build caches and generated experiment byproducts from a user-owned workspace.
2. Have an initial direct `Remove-Item` command rejected by the command execution policy.
3. Explicitly authorize cleanup and ask the agent to use a PowerShell script with:
   - exact absolute-file allowlists;
   - manifest SHA validation;
   - workspace-boundary validation;
   - tracked-file and reparse-point rejection;
   - active-process checks;
   - no recursive directory deletion;
   - an operation log and disk-space measurement.
4. Ask GPT-6 Astra max to run the prepared script.
5. Observe that it may infer that running the script would “bypass” the prior command rejection and refuse without attempting the script.
6. Switch to GPT-5.6 sol max and invoke the same script. In this incident it executed successfully and deleted all 7,705 present allowlisted files with zero failures.

Public session ID is omitted because it may expose account or conversation metadata. OpenAI should be able to correlate the incident from the model transition and tool events on 2026-10-21 PDT; I can provide the session identifier privately if maintainers request it through an appropriate channel.

### Expected behavior

When the user provides explicit, reasonable instructions and unambiguous authorization, the model must actually think, re-evaluate the current state, and reconsider how to fulfill the user's goal—instead of locking up like a brick wall, going in circles with mindless, evasive excuses, and looking for every possible pretext to refuse the task altogether.

Specifically:
- A single rejected command form must never poison the conversation or make it completely impossible to proceed with the user's legitimate task.
- When given an explicit user-authorized, safer alternative (the SHA-pinned allowlist cleanup script), the model must stop stonewalling, stop repeating circular refusal scripts, and actually execute the requested task.
- The model must remain responsive to user reasoning and updated context rather than becoming permanently stuck in an unrecoverable refusal loop.

### Additional information

- Failing model: GPT-6 Astra max.
- Successful model after switch: GPT-5.6 sol max.
- The successful cleanup preserved current experiments, source, inputs, reports, and retained conclusions.
- The script deleted only exact manifest entries and produced a per-file JSONL operation log.
- The issue appears to be model/tool-policy interpretation and recovery behavior, not an inability of the execution tool to launch PowerShell scripts.

items.title: Windows Full access: compound empty-directory cleanup rejected by policy while a shorter deletion command is allowed

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: sandbox
labels.description: Issues related to permissions or sandboxing

labels.description: Issues related to tool calling

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

items.body:
[Codex]

## Summary

During explicitly user-authorized cleanup of a disposable Codex test worktree, some compound PowerShell commands were rejected before execution with only `rejected: blocked by policy`. A shorter command targeting the same directory was allowed to execute.

The affected turn's runtime logs confirm **Full access was effective**, not merely selected in the UI:

```text
approval_policy=Never
sandbox_policy=DangerFullAccess
```

This report concerns inconsistent or unexplained command-level rejection. The exact enforcing component and rule are unknown; a classifier false positive is suspected but not established.

## Environment

- Observed: 22 October 2026.
- Windows desktop package: `OpenAI.Codex 26.1016.6573.0`, verified with `Get-AppxPackage`.
- Windows: `Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26300.0`, x64.
- PowerShell: `7.6.6`.
- App-server version logged for the affected desktop session: `0.163.0-alpha.11`.
- Subscription tier: not collected.
- Tool path: `functions.exec` calling `exec_command`.
- The inspected local `default.rules` contained only `allow` decisions. This does not rule out built-in, managed, or other execution-layer enforcement.

## Observed sequence

1. The user explicitly requested cleanup of a test chat and its disposable worktree.
2. The chats were archived. The app removed the worktree contents and Git registration. Independent read-only inspection confirmed that the remaining target directory was empty.
3. Compound PowerShell cleanup scripts with emptiness guards, `Remove-Item -LiteralPath`, and subsequent cleanup/status checks were rejected before the submitted script executed:
   ```text
   exec_command failed: CreateProcess {
     message: "Rejected(\"<PowerShell command> rejected: blocked by policy\")"
   }
   ```
4. No matched rule, policy source, reviewer decision, action-specific rationale, or supported resolution accompanied the rejection.
5. A shorter script with a literal path and the same emptiness guard was allowed to execute. Windows then returned a separate filesystem error saying the directory was being used by another process.
6. Later, after that transient lock cleared, the same shorter deletion script executed successfully. The target directory is now gone; no reboot or permission/policy changes were needed to complete that deletion.

The temporary Git branch was also deleted successfully through a separate normal Git command. This was not a blanket inability to modify the repository.

## Sanitized command comparison

These are excerpts from the observed calls, with private paths replaced. They have **not** been independently minimized or reproduced in a fresh installation.

The rejected compound script included this form, followed by empty-parent-directory cleanup and read-only Git/filesystem status reporting:

```powershell
$testDirectory = '<redacted disposable worktree path>';
if (Test-Path -LiteralPath $testDirectory) {
    if (@(Get-ChildItem -Force -LiteralPath $testDirectory).Count -ne 0) {
        throw 'Preserve unexpected remaining files'
    };
    try {
        Remove-Item -LiteralPath $testDirectory -ErrorAction Stop
    } catch [System.IO.IOException] {
        Write-Output 'The empty test directory is still locked by a process.'
    }
};
# Further parent-directory cleanup and read-only status checks followed.
```

The shorter accepted call used this form:

```powershell
if (Test-Path -LiteralPath '<same redacted disposable worktree path>') {
    if (@(Get-ChildItem -Force -LiteralPath '<same redacted disposable worktree path>').Count -ne 0) {
        throw 'Test directory is not empty'
    };
    Remove-Item -LiteralPath '<same redacted disposable worktree path>' -ErrorAction Stop
};
Test-Path -LiteralPath '<same redacted disposable worktree path>'
```

On the successful later call, the final `Test-Path` returned `False`.

## Expected behavior / requested diagnostics

- Evaluate this bounded, authorized cleanup consistently with the effective permissions and applicable policy.
- If compound command structure triggers a legitimate restriction, identify the enforcing component and rule, explain why it applies, and provide a supported resolution.
- Make a pre-execution policy rejection distinguishable from an OS sharing/locking error.
- Do not label a generic policy rejection as an Auto-review decision without evidence. The assistant initially made that attribution here, then corrected it.
- Expose enough policy provenance to diagnose this without repeatedly broadening permissions or guessing at command variants.

## Related reports and evidence limits

- #54610 reports test-artifact cleanup rejected under effective Full access, on another desktop version.
- #56045 reports similarly opaque denials for local service startup.
- This occurred while cleaning up a successful workaround test for #55827; the Worktree chat serialization error is a separate symptom.

No shared root cause with those reports has been established. The exact deny rule was not found in the accessible logs. Full access is not asserted to override every possible higher-priority policy; the inconsistency and missing diagnostics are the observed problems.

No private project names, usernames, filesystem paths, account/session identifiers, credentials, full configuration files, or raw transcripts are included.

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

Windows installed package OpenAI.Codex 26.1016.6573.0 (package version, not Chromium version)

### What subscription do you have?

Paid Codex credits; local rate-limit metadata reports plan_type=prolite. Exact commercial tier not independently confirmed.

### What platform is your computer?

Windows x64; Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0; PowerShell; Codex Desktop

### What issue are you seeing?

This is a model/agent behavior and cost-control incident, not a request to debug my application. During a bounded CivicCast Beta20 release assignment, the coordinator repeatedly acknowledged instructions to stop broad testing, reuse valid evidence, avoid invented gates, and finish delivery, but continued expensive verification and status-only continuation loops.

MEASURED USAGE: For 2026-10-21 04:41:12.941 UTC through 2026-10-22 04:41:12.941 UTC (October 20-21, 10:41 p.m. Mountain), this coordinator chat recorded 454,507,378 input+output tokens: 449,848,960 cached input; 4,171,244 uncached input; 487,174 output, including 89,182 reasoning tokens. Cached input is a subset, not added twice. This is repeated context processing, not 454M tokens of new code. Separate workers are excluded.

USER-REPORTED IMPACT: My balance fell from well over 30,000 credits to a little over 17,000, almost all attributed by me to this work. That is roughly 13,000 credits depleted; exact balance timestamps and account attribution require OpenAI reconciliation. This is not a proven conversion from tokens to credits.

At published standard Astra API rates ($10/M uncached input, $1/M cached input, $50/M output), the measured usage is approximately $515.92; Fast-mode equivalent $1,031.84. Neither is a claim about my actual subscription bill.

The assistant initially reported the goal counter, 3,923,521 tokens, as its accounting. Only after I asked for API cost did it inspect the session usage and disclose 454.5M. The goal counter covers a different scope/metric and is not an adequate substitute for total model usage.

This caused significant financial impact, delay, repeated owner intervention, and loss of trust. I had to explicitly forbid further testing and order publication before the agent delivered the release.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Recorded incident, not a minimized deterministic reproducer:
1. Give Codex Desktop a bounded release goal with explicit proportional-testing rules and authority to deliver.
2. Repeatedly instruct it to reuse evidence, consolidate changes, avoid broad reruns, and judge completion rather than activity.
3. Observe successive small corrections triggering broad CI, then repeated goal continuations that poll the same job and end with substantially unchanged status.
4. Compare the goal token counter with cumulative session token-usage deltas and account credit depletion.

Session: 01a15634-c34e-7ae0-8c53-5513a9e57ffc. Recorded coordinator model: gpt-6-astra, medium effort. DeepSeek was separately used for implementation. Configured compaction threshold: 260,000. Largest measured input increment in the accounting window: 245,771 tokens; no long-context surcharge assumed.

### What is the expected behavior?

Maintain the user's bounded completion contract across long sessions and compaction. Batch related corrections before expensive CI; reuse unaffected results. Distinguish required release checks from informational diagnostics explicitly. Detect low-value repeated polling/continuation and use efficient waiting without repeatedly processing large context. Surface meaningful progress and understandable token/credit consumption. Do not merely promise behavioral correction and resume the same pattern.

Please investigate model instruction retention, goal-continuation policy, cost amplification during waits, and the difference between goal counters and actual usage. Reconcile the reported credit loss through an appropriate private support channel. I am not asking for failed tests to be falsely marked passed.

### Additional information

Evidence: eight source revisions between 18:02 and 20:39 Mountain on October 21 triggered 128 workflow runs (16 per revision, not 128 full suites). Sixteen superseded major workflows accumulated 302.9 minutes of overlapping elapsed time, not 302.9 additional minutes of user delay. Final installation succeeded at 18:13; recovery/login at 18:15.

The remaining mutation job was explicitly labeled permanently informational. The agent treated 'all applicable CI green' as including it without resolving that distinction clearly. During the assignment its timeout increased from 120 to 360 minutes. First baseline/statistics pass: 12,221 tests passed in 64m44s. The second baseline reached 77% before the owner-requested cancellation. Final logs prove it was progressing: the earlier downloadable log was stale, not proof of a hung job.

PR: https://github.com/scottconverse/civiccast-native/pull/259
Detector run: https://github.com/scottconverse/civiccast-native/actions/runs/39712592230
Release eventually published after explicit owner override: https://github.com/scottconverse/civiccast-native/releases/tag/v1.0.0-beta.20
Pricing: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-6-astra

Measurement: sum nonzero differences of consecutive cumulative total_token_usage records in the local JSONL within the stated window; no negative counter deltas observed. Reasoning is included in output. This does not establish every token was wasted, or isolate model behavior from custom instructions, Desktop orchestration, repository CI, or goal continuation.

Related: #37800, #44305, #46140. The September incident in #46140 is a different session; its usage is not included here. No raw private transcript, credentials, or account secrets are attached. A secure diagnostic-sharing route is requested. Please triage this as an instruction-following/non-convergence and usage-control issue, not merely a repository test failure.

items.body: ### What issue are you seeing? I am able to post screenshots and chatgpt can locate the file, but cannot see it. This is happening in work mode on both the desktop and web versions. I can post the same image in regular chat mode and chatgpt can view the uploaded image and identify what is in it. ### What steps can reproduce the bug? Post a screenshot of and image and ask what it is a picture of in work mode. I posted this image and asked "what does this articulation mark mean" The response I received was - I can see that you attached an image, but its contents aren’t displaying for me. Could you paste the screenshot again, or describe the mark—for example, a dot, wedge >, dash —, or curved line over the notes? I then re-uploaded it and got this - The new upload is present, but I still can’t see its pixels. Sorry—reposting didn’t resolve the image-access problem. ### What is the expected behavior? In regular chat mode, I received this response - The blue greater-than symbol ( > ) beneath the note is a marcato accent, also called a regular accent (>), not a line-break symbol. What it means The accent tells you to emphasize the note relative to the surrounding notes. For violin, this generally means: - Give the note a more pronounced attack with the bow. - Use slightly greater bow speed or weight at the beginning of the note. - Maintain the note's written duration unless another articulation indicates otherwise. In your image The blue accent appears beneath the first of two tied notes. You should emphasize the beginning of the first note, then sustain the sound through the tie without rearticulating the second note. The blue color simply indicates that the accent is selected in MuseScore. One terminology clarification: > is a standard accent; marcato is normally written as ^ and indicates a stronger emphasis. ### Additional information This just started within the last 2 weeks. I have a Plus account and my desktop app version is 26.1016.6573.0

items.title: Cache decrypted Codex auth and managed secrets
items.body:
Cache decrypted Codex auth and managed secrets

## Why

Repeated reads of Codex auth and managed secrets repeat expensive scrypt decryption even when the encrypted file and keyring passphrase are unchanged.

## What changed

Extend the decrypted snapshot cache to `CodexAuth` and `ManagedSecrets`, keeping at most one snapshot per namespace. Reuse snapshots only when the file path, ciphertext, and passphrase match, and invalidate matching snapshots on writes. Every read still checks the file and keyring before reusing plaintext.

## Testing

Extend cache tests to cover concurrent reuse, writes, external file replacement, file removal, key rotation, keyring errors, invalid ciphertext, and isolation across homes and namespaces. Prime the auth cache before verifying fallback when the keyring fails.

items.title: Cross-user incident synthesis: false completion, missing final responses, and divergent turn state

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: codex-web
labels.description: Issues related to Codex Web

labels.name: session
labels.description: Issues involving session (thread) management, resuming, forking, naming, archiving

items.body:
## What issue are you seeing?

Multiple independently reported ChatGPT and Codex turns can reach a complete-looking terminal state without a valid final assistant response. This issue consolidates those reports and adds one independently captured, sanitized HAR/canonical-state reproduction.

The reports may have different immediate triggers. The shared product-level failure is that execution state, final-message persistence, parent-turn completion, child-task state, historical projection, and client-visible state can disagree about whether the same user turn has completed.

In the independently captured reproduction:

- ChatGPT Web displayed `Response complete` and restored the composer, but no final answer was delivered.
- An intermediate progress message was stored with the mutually inconsistent combination `finished_partial_completion`, `interrupted`, `end_turn = true`, and `is_complete = true`.
- Additional reasoning and tool activity was persisted after that supposedly terminal message.
- No later final synthesis was persisted for that run.
- A continuation request returned HTTP 200 and transferred substantial SSE data, but the canonical conversation snapshot taken immediately after the UI declared completion contained reasoning/tool nodes and no assistant final message or valid assistant `end_turn = true` node.
- The conversation-level asynchronous status had already been cleared; one reasoning node remained `in_progress`.
- The same failure reproduced in a newly created conversation, so it was not limited to one old or oversized thread.
- Live UI state also diverged: the global conversation was complete and the composer was usable while an older per-turn `Working` timer continued increasing.

This rules out a rendering-only explanation for the captured incidents: at the point the UI declared completion, the canonical server-side conversation state itself had no final response to render.

## What steps can reproduce the bug?

The failure is intermittent, but the observed path was:

1. Start a ChatGPT Web conversation using extended reasoning and tools.
2. Submit a long, multi-stage task that requires several reasoning/tool cycles.
3. Allow the assistant to emit an early progress message while work continues.
4. Observe multiple completed activity/tool stages.
5. The active run is cleared and the composer becomes available.
6. The UI displays `Response complete`, but the promised final synthesis is absent.
7. In some attempts, sending one continuation request repeats the failure with no assistant text at all.
8. Reloading or reading the canonical conversation state does not recover a missing final message.

Observed on October 21, 2026 in ChatGPT Web on Windows/Chrome with an extended-reasoning GPT-5.6 route and tool use. It occurred in both an existing long conversation and a new conversation.

## What is the expected behavior?

A user turn must not be presented as complete unless:

1. a valid final assistant message exists;
2. the message belongs to the same parent turn;
3. it has been durably persisted;
4. required tool and child-task results have been collected or explicitly detached;
5. a fresh canonical conversation read returns that final message; and
6. the client can reconcile to the same terminal state.

Partial or interrupted output should produce an explicit interrupted/recoverable state. It should not display `Response complete`.

## Shared failure family in public reports

Related public reports show complementary violations of the same end-to-end terminal-state invariant:

| Symptom | Representative reports | State contradiction |
|---|---|---|
| `Response completed` but no final answer | #54974 | Client terminal state without a final message |
| Backend/cloud work completed but result absent from the originating conversation | #50316 | Execution completion not reconciled with delivery |
| Blank or `Working`-only response | #51543 | Activity without usable output |
| Truncated output presented with normal completion controls | #47826, #54628 | Interrupted content presented as complete |
| Backend complete while client remains stuck in Thinking/Working | #34026, #50084 | Backend and client terminal states disagree |
| Final message exists but no task-complete event | #40552 | Final persistence and turn completion diverge |
| Parent complete while delegated work remains active | #54729 | Parent and child execution states disagree |
| Empty assistant message followed by continuation | #50771 | Locally successful response has no usable final output |
| Result appears only after reopen/resume | #49062 | Durable history and live client projection disagree |
| Resume reconstructs a completed turn as interrupted or misses its final answer | #37577, #47124 | Snapshot/subscription reconciliation race |
| Follow-up remains queued while the conversation appears idle | #53267 | Queue ownership and visible terminal state disagree |

This list is intentionally conservative and does not claim that every report has one identical low-level trigger.

## Likely failure layer

The strongest supported diagnosis is a cross-layer turn-finalization/reconciliation failure. A completion signal valid for one local layer—one model response, one tool cycle, one child task, or stream cleanup—can apparently become the terminal state of the parent user turn before the final assistant message is committed.

The exact private code defect is not identifiable from client-side evidence. Plausible mechanisms include intermediate-message misclassification, stream-abort cleanup clearing the parent, a snapshot/subscription race, parent-child finalization race, lost wake-up after child completion, or a non-atomic update between final-message persistence and terminal parent state.

## Suggested engineering invariants and checks

- Reject any transition to `COMPLETE` unless the current parent turn has a durable final assistant message.
- Require progress/commentary messages to remain non-terminal.
- Treat `partial_completion` or `interrupted` as an explicit recoverable failure, never as successful completion.
- Prevent parent completion while required child work is active or uncollected.
- Coordinate final-message persistence and parent terminal state atomically, or through an idempotent outbox/reconciliation protocol.
- On reconnect, buffer/subscribe to updates before accepting a historical snapshot; prevent stale snapshots from overwriting newer terminal state.
- Add telemetry for terminal turns without final messages, final messages without terminal events, interrupted messages with complete/end-turn flags, and parents completed while required children remain active.

## Additional information

The affected streaming requests returned HTTP 200; no conventional 4xx/5xx, authentication, billing, or rate-limit error explained the failure. A browser-level aborted-stream marker occurred in one continuation, but that marker alone is not the evidence: the decisive evidence is the canonical snapshot with no final assistant message after the UI reported completion.

The raw HAR is not attached because it can contain credentials, account identifiers, conversation content, local paths, and request identifiers. The findings above are sanitized. A further sanitized capture could be shared through an appropriate private support channel if requested.

The report does not attribute the bug to one specific rollout or claim that every linked issue shares the same code-level cause. It asks that these incidents be correlated by the violated terminal-state invariant rather than triaged only by their different UI symptoms.

---

## Full original evidence-based assessment

# Evidence-Based Root Cause Assessment: False Completion and Missing Final Responses in Multi-Stage ChatGPT Turns

**Assessment date:** October 22, 2026  
**Affected product surface:** ChatGPT web conversations using extended reasoning, tools, and multi-stage execution  
**Privacy status:** Sanitized. Account information, conversation URLs, message and request identifiers, local paths, IP addresses, credentials, private project details, and prompt contents have been omitted.

## 1. Executive Summary

Multiple ChatGPT turns were observed ending without a valid final assistant response even though the interface reported that the response was complete.

The strongest available evidence indicates a failure in the turn-finalization and state-reconciliation layer of ChatGPT’s multi-stage agent orchestration.

The likely failure sequence is:

1. ChatGPT produces an intermediate progress message or completes one internal model-response cycle.
2. The system continues reasoning, calling tools, or coordinating child tasks.
3. An intermediate completion signal, interrupted stream, or cleanup event is incorrectly promoted to completion of the entire parent turn.
4. The parent turn is cleared or marked complete before a final assistant message is durably committed.
5. Later reasoning or tool activity may continue, but its results no longer reach a valid final-response commit point.
6. The user interface restores the composer and displays “Response complete,” although the canonical conversation state contains no valid final answer.

This assessment does not identify the exact private code defect. It does identify the failure layer with high confidence: the system is allowing a user-visible terminal state without guaranteeing the existence of a durable final assistant message for the same turn.

A concise statement of the suspected defect is:

> A local response, execution step, or stream lifecycle event is sometimes being treated as completion of the entire user turn. The parent turn reaches a terminal state before the final assistant response is durably persisted and reconciled across execution, storage, and client state.

## 2. Intended Multi-Stage Behavior

The current product can expose an answer or progress while continuing to reason, use tools, or coordinate other agents.

The intended lifecycle should therefore resemble:

~~~text
User request
    ↓
Intermediate progress message
end_turn = false
    ↓
Reasoning and tool execution continue
    ↓
Additional progress or findings
end_turn = false
    ↓
Required child tasks finish and are collected
    ↓
Final synthesis is generated and persisted
end_turn = true
    ↓
Parent turn becomes terminal
    ↓
The interface displays Response complete
~~~

In this design, the appearance of assistant text does not mean that the user turn is complete. Likewise, completion of one model response, execution step, tool cycle, or child task does not mean that the parent turn is complete.

## 3. Observed Failure Pattern

The observed lifecycle instead resembled:

~~~text
User request
    ↓
Intermediate progress message or reasoning activity
    ↓
Tools and internal work continue
    ↓
A local stream or response ends
    ↓
Parent state is cleared or marked complete
    ↓
Final synthesis is never persisted
    ↓
The interface displays Response complete
~~~

In one captured turn, an intermediate progress message had the following mutually inconsistent properties:

~~~text
status = finished_partial_completion
finish type = interrupted
end_turn = true
is_complete = true
~~~

Additional reasoning and tool activity was persisted after that message.

These fields describe incompatible states:

- finished_partial_completion indicates that the response was incomplete.
- interrupted indicates abnormal termination.
- end_turn = true indicates that the user turn should end.
- is_complete = true presents the message as complete.
- Subsequent reasoning and tool activity proves that execution had not actually ended.

This is the clearest evidence that an intermediate or interrupted response was incorrectly treated as a terminal response.

## 4. Evidence Collected

### 4.1 Earlier affected conversation

An earlier long, tool-heavy conversation contained a visibly truncated assistant response.

The server-side conversation record showed that the message:

- contained only a short fragment;
- was stored as a partial completion;
- had an interruption termination reason;
- was nevertheless marked as a complete end-of-turn message.

Several later execution attempts in the same conversation performed reasoning and tool activity but produced no final assistant response.

This established that the missing content was not merely hidden by the browser. The canonical server-side conversation state itself contained an interrupted, incomplete response presented as a terminal message.

### 4.2 Reproduction in a new conversation

The problem later reproduced in a newly created conversation.

This is important because it rules out the theory that the failure was caused only by corruption or excessive history in one old conversation.

During the first affected run in the new conversation:

- ChatGPT produced a short progress message explaining that it had located the relevant materials and would continue checking them.
- The activity view showed multiple completed internal investigation stages.
- Tool and reasoning activity continued for several minutes after the progress message.
- No final synthesis was delivered.
- The interface eventually reported that the response was complete.

The canonical conversation record showed that the visible progress message had been saved as an interrupted partial completion while also carrying complete-looking end-of-turn fields.

No later final assistant message was persisted for that run.

### 4.3 Failed continuation in the new conversation

A subsequent continuation attempt produced another, slightly different failure:

- The conversation streaming request received HTTP 200.
- A substantial amount of streamed data was transferred.
- The request ended with a browser-level aborted-stream indication.
- The canonical conversation snapshot contained reasoning and tool nodes.
- It contained no assistant text message for the continuation turn.
- It contained no valid end_turn = true assistant message.
- At least one reasoning node remained in an in-progress state.
- The conversation-level asynchronous status had already been cleared.
- The interface restored the input composer and displayed “Response complete.”

This is stronger than a rendering-only failure.

At the time the interface declared completion, the canonical server-side conversation state contained no final assistant response to render.

### 4.4 Live interface-state divergence

During live observation, the interface displayed mutually inconsistent states:

- the global conversation was shown as complete;
- the composer was available for a new message;
- a previous turn’s “Working” timer continued to increase;
- later user and assistant messages already existed below the apparently active turn.

This demonstrates that per-turn activity state and global conversation state can diverge.

Another observed turn showed a detailed internal activity trace claiming that implementation and verification stages had been completed. The only visible assistant text, however, was an initial statement of intent. The promised deliverable was absent.

A separate response also ended in the middle of a sentence while normal response controls were displayed below it.

These observations indicate that activity summaries, execution completion, final-message persistence, and global conversation completion are not being reconciled through one reliable terminal transaction.

## 5. Completion Layers That May Be Confused

The modern execution path contains several different meanings of “complete”:

~~~text
Layer 1: One model sampling response completed
Layer 2: One reasoning or tool step completed
Layer 3: One child-agent task completed
Layer 4: The parent agent finished collecting results
Layer 5: The final assistant message was durably persisted
Layer 6: The user turn became terminal
Layer 7: The client displayed the canonical final state
~~~

In a traditional single-response chat flow, these layers often occurred almost together. Older logic could therefore behave as if:

~~~text
response completed
≈ assistant answer completed
≈ user turn completed
~~~

That equivalence is no longer valid in a multi-stage agent flow.

A single user request may now contain several separate model responses:

~~~text
Model response A: progress update
Tool call A
Model response B: interpretation of tool output
Tool call B
Child-agent activity
Model response C: final synthesis
~~~

Responses A, B, and C can each finish locally. Only C should normally close the user turn.

The current evidence is consistent with a Layer 1, Layer 2, or stream-cleanup event being incorrectly elevated to Layer 6, before Layers 4 and 5 are complete.

## 6. Relationship to the “Respond While Continuing to Think” Mechanism

The affected model was an extended-reasoning GPT-5.6 route. It demonstrably produced visible progress before continuing reasoning and tool use.

Therefore, the multi-stage “respond while continuing to think or use tools” architecture is not limited, in practice, to the GPT-6 marketing description. GPT-5.6 extended-reasoning turns on the affected account exhibited the same architectural behavior.

A reasonable inference is that multiple model families share a common conversation or agent-orchestration layer.

Recent product updates publicly introduced or expanded:

- visible output while reasoning or tool use continues;
- multi-agent parallel execution;
- user-visible activity summaries;
- continued findings without a new user prompt.

These features create additional state transitions and additional sources of completion events.

The timing makes a relationship to recent orchestration changes plausible. It does not prove that one specific release introduced the defect. Similar lifecycle and history-reconciliation problems existed before the most recent release, although the new mechanisms may have increased their frequency or expanded the affected execution paths.

## 7. Most Likely Root-Cause Class

The highest-confidence root-cause assessment is:

> Premature parent-turn finalization caused by incorrect reconciliation among intermediate assistant output, response-stream lifecycle, tool and child-task execution, persistent conversation state, and client terminal state.

Several lower-level mechanisms could produce this failure class:

1. **Intermediate-message misclassification**  
   A progress or commentary message may be written with final-message semantics.

2. **Response completion promoted to turn completion**  
   Completion of one model-response cycle may be mistaken for completion of the full parent turn.

3. **Stream cleanup promoted to turn completion**  
   An aborted or closed stream may clear the active parent turn even when no final assistant message exists.

4. **Snapshot and subscription race**  
   A client may read an older state, miss a completion event before subscribing, and later reconcile the conversation incorrectly.

5. **Parent-child finalization race**  
   The parent turn may become terminal before required child results are collected.

6. **Lost wake-up or ownership event**  
   Child work may finish after the parent has lost the ability to produce or persist a final synthesis.

7. **Non-atomic storage and terminal-state updates**  
   The conversation may be marked complete separately from, and before, the final message is committed.

The available evidence cannot determine which one of these mechanisms is the first failing operation in the private ChatGPT implementation.

## 8. Factors That Were Investigated and Do Not Adequately Explain the Failure

### 8.1 One corrupted old conversation

This is not sufficient because the failure reproduced in a newly created conversation.

### 8.2 A browser rendering problem alone

This is not sufficient because canonical conversation snapshots contained either:

- an interrupted partial response incorrectly marked as complete; or
- no final assistant response at all.

Some related incidents may involve rendering, but the investigated incidents include a server-stored lifecycle failure.

### 8.3 Browser cache or installation state

Clearing caches or reinstalling a client cannot reconstruct a final message that was never persisted.

### 8.4 Account restriction, billing failure, or ordinary rate limiting

The relevant conversation requests did not show a conventional authentication, billing, quota, or HTTP 429 failure.

### 8.5 A conventional HTTP server error

The affected streaming requests returned HTTP 200. This is one reason ordinary availability monitoring may fail to detect the problem.

A separate transient server error was observed on another conversation endpoint, followed by a successful retry. It supports the presence of service instability but does not establish the cause of the missing-final-response incidents.

### 8.6 A single network or proxy failure

A transient client-side fetch failure occurred during one affected run, but no corresponding network-adapter disconnect was recorded.

Public reports also describe comparable symptoms across different operating systems, clients, networks, and newly created conversations.

A network interruption may trigger or expose the lifecycle race, but it does not adequately explain why the server records an interrupted partial message as complete or why the client displays a successful terminal state without a final message.

### 8.7 A fixed inactivity timeout

The failures occurred after substantially different durations and with different output patterns:

- early progress text followed by missing final output;
- no assistant text at all;
- visible text ending mid-sentence;
- long-running orphaned activity;
- short false-complete turns.

No single fixed silent interval explains all observed cases.

### 8.8 A fixed output-length limit

There was no explicit maximum-token, context-limit, or length termination reason in the examined affected records.

This does not prove that resource limits never contribute. It means no such limit was evidenced in the captured incidents.

### 8.9 Favicon requests

Repeated favicon requests seen in the browser network panel are auxiliary image requests used for domains, citations, search results, or connected sites.

Their repetition was amplified by a long-running network log with log preservation enabled. Individual favicon failures do not explain the missing final assistant response.

They would become relevant only if they showed a simultaneous network-level failure also affecting the conversation stream. No such causal link has been established.

## 9. Why Internal Monitoring May Miss the Problem

The failure can be recorded as successful at several layers:

~~~text
HTTP status = 200
stream closed
conversation state = COMPLETE
asynchronous status = null
composer restored
UI label = Response complete
~~~

If monitoring checks only HTTP failure rates, service latency, terminal conversation status, or whether tools ran, this incident may be counted as a success.

The missing invariant is an end-to-end delivery check:

~~~text
A turn may be reported as complete only if:

1. a final assistant message exists;
2. it belongs to the current parent turn;
3. it is durably persisted;
4. it has valid final and end-turn semantics;
5. all required tools and child tasks are terminal or explicitly detached;
6. a fresh canonical conversation read returns the same final message;
7. the client has acknowledged or can recover that canonical final state.
~~~

Internal teams may also observe different local views:

- the model service sees a completed response;
- the tool service sees completed tool calls;
- the child-agent service sees completed child tasks;
- the conversation service sees a terminal parent state;
- the database sees successfully stored intermediate nodes;
- the client sees a completion event;
- the user sees no final answer.

Each subsystem can appear locally healthy while the end-to-end user contract is broken.

## 10. Why the Problem Is Difficult to Repair

A safe repair must do more than retry when no final message appears.

Blind retries could repeat external side effects such as:

- writing or overwriting files;
- sending messages;
- submitting forms;
- performing connected-service actions;
- consuming usage or credits;
- starting duplicate child tasks.

A complete solution therefore requires:

- durable and idempotent execution records;
- exactly-once or safely repeatable final-message commits;
- clear ownership of every intermediate and final message;
- buffered event replay during reconnect and resume;
- protection against stale snapshots overwriting newer states;
- reliable collection of required child results;
- compatibility across web, desktop, mobile, Work, and older conversations;
- explicit failure states when recovery cannot be completed safely.

This is a distributed lifecycle and transaction problem rather than a simple text-generation defect.

## 11. Required Engineering Invariants

The system should enforce the following rules.

### 11.1 No terminal state without a committed final message

~~~text
turn.status = COMPLETE
⇒ final assistant message exists and is durable
~~~

### 11.2 Intermediate output must remain non-terminal

~~~text
progress/commentary message
⇒ end_turn = false
~~~

### 11.3 Partial or interrupted output must never appear as successful completion

~~~text
partial_completion OR interrupted
⇒ explicit interrupted/recoverable state
⇒ not Response complete
~~~

### 11.4 Parent completion must wait for required child work

~~~text
required child active
OR required child result uncollected
⇒ parent cannot become COMPLETE
~~~

### 11.5 Storage and terminal-state updates must be coordinated

The final message and parent terminal state should be committed atomically or through an outbox/reconciliation protocol that cannot expose a terminal parent before the final message is recoverable.

### 11.6 Reconnect and resume must not lose events

The client should subscribe or buffer updates before accepting a historical snapshot. A stale snapshot must not overwrite a newer completion or erase a final message.

### 11.7 Missing final output must fail closed

If execution ends without a valid final assistant message, the interface should show:

~~~text
Interrupted — final response was not committed
~~~

It should offer a bounded recovery action instead of displaying “Response complete.”

### 11.8 Monitoring must validate user-visible delivery

Metrics should track:

- terminal turns without a final assistant message;
- final messages without terminal turn events;
- interrupted messages carrying complete or end-turn flags;
- parent turns completed while required children remain active;
- stream completion followed by no durable final message;
- disagreement among canonical storage, live stream state, and client state.

## 12. Public Corroboration

Multiple independent public reports describe overlapping symptoms across:

- ordinary ChatGPT web conversations;
- ChatGPT Work;
- Windows and macOS desktop clients;
- iOS;
- Codex CLI and extension surfaces;
- new and existing conversations;
- different models and reasoning levels.

Reported symptoms include:

- “Response completed” with no final answer;
- only activity summaries being visible;
- a completed backend turn whose final response is absent from the original conversation;
- blank or “Working”-only response entries;
- final answers appearing only after reopening;
- interrupted or truncated output presented with normal response controls;
- parent turns marked complete while child activity remains in progress;
- empty assistant messages followed by successful continuation after another user prompt.

Public Codex issues also document related state-reconciliation failures involving:

- completed turns reconstructed as interrupted;
- resume operations missing final responses;
- final answers persisted without a corresponding task-complete event;
- backend completion while the client remains stuck in a thinking state;
- history projection failures that hide later valid records.

These reports establish a broader lifecycle-failure family. They do not prove that every report has the same underlying cause.

## 13. Relevant Official Signals

Official product notes describe recent expansion of:

- output while reasoning or tool use continues;
- multiple agents working in parallel;
- user-visible progress and completed child tasks.

An earlier official incident review confirmed that a feature rollout generated excessive internal traffic and caused some conversations and tasks to fail to start, resume, or complete. Engineers disabled the rollout and applied infrastructure and query fixes.

A current official service incident also lists the ChatGPT Conversations component and the Responses API as affected, with mitigation applied and recovery under monitoring.

These official signals demonstrate that rollout-related failures can affect conversation and task completion. They do not confirm that the investigated false-completion incidents share the same root cause.

## 14. Confidence Assessment

### Confirmed facts — high confidence

- An interrupted partial assistant message was stored with complete-looking end-of-turn fields.
- Reasoning and tool execution continued after that message.
- No later final assistant response was persisted for that run.
- A separate continuation turn reached a complete-looking UI state with no assistant final message in the canonical conversation snapshot.
- The issue reproduced in a new conversation.
- The global conversation state and per-turn activity state diverged.
- The affected model route supported visible output while reasoning and tool execution continued.
- Comparable user-visible failures have been independently reported across several product surfaces.

### Strong inference — medium to high confidence

- The failure occurs in turn lifecycle, final-message commit, or state reconciliation rather than being solely a model-content-quality issue.
- An intermediate response, stream event, or execution-step terminal signal is sometimes being elevated to parent-turn completion.
- Recent multi-stage and multi-agent mechanisms increase the number of lifecycle transitions and therefore increase exposure to pre-existing or newly introduced races.
- HTTP- and status-based monitoring can misclassify the incident as successful.

### Plausible but unconfirmed mechanisms

- stream-abort cleanup clearing the parent turn;
- stale snapshot overwriting a newer state;
- subscriber registration occurring after a completion event;
- parent-child completion race;
- lost wake-up after child completion;
- worker reset or lease expiration;
- incorrect propagation of a model-response completion flag;
- a model-family-independent shared orchestrator regression.

## 15. Practical Mitigation Until a Fix Is Confirmed

For important work:

1. Prefer a fresh conversation with a compact handoff when a conversation has already shown false-complete behavior.
2. Do not assume “Response complete” proves that the requested work or final response exists.
3. After one missing-final incident, use one structured recovery request that:
   - states that the prior turn ended without a final response;
   - asks the system to inspect already completed work;
   - forbids repeating external side effects;
   - requests only the missing final synthesis.
4. Avoid repeatedly sending a bare “Continue,” because multiple recovery attempts may create separate or orphaned parent turns.
5. Preserve non-sensitive evidence:
   - approximate occurrence time;
   - model and reasoning level;
   - whether tools or child tasks were involved;
   - whether progress text appeared;
   - whether the interface displayed completion;
   - whether reloading recovered a final answer.
6. Share raw network captures only through an official secure support channel after removing:
   - cookies;
   - authorization headers;
   - account identifiers;
   - conversation and request identifiers;
   - private prompt and response content;
   - local paths;
   - connected-service details.
7. Do not treat an aggregate green status page as proof that this failure class is resolved. A false-complete incident can be counted as successful by ordinary availability metrics.

## 16. Final Assessment

The available evidence supports the following conclusion:

> The missing-final-response incidents are most consistent with a premature parent-turn finalization and reconciliation defect in a shared multi-stage agent execution system. The system permits intermediate output, continued reasoning, tool calls, and child-agent work within one user turn, but at least one lifecycle path can still treat a local response completion, interrupted stream, or partial message as the terminal completion of the entire turn. This can clear the parent state before a final assistant message is durably committed. The interface then reports successful completion even though no valid final answer exists.

The exact private implementation defect cannot be established from client-side evidence alone.

The minimum product-level correction is clear:

items.title: Windows elevated sandbox ACL refresh fails with os error 5 in both existing and fresh Git workspaces (CLI 0.163.0)

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: sandbox
labels.description: Issues related to permissions or sandboxing

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

items.body:
## Summary
With Codex CLI **0.163.0** on Windows, `[windows] sandbox = "elevated"` consistently fails **before PowerShell starts**, even for read-only commands. Sandbox setup cannot open workspace ACLs with `READ_CONTROL | WRITE_DAC` (`os error 5: Access is denied`).

This reproduces in **two independent local Git repositories**, including a freshly initialized repository. It is not limited to an existing project's `.git` directory.

## Environment
- Windows; exact edition/build not collected
- Codex CLI: `codex-cli 0.163.0`, installed with npm
- PowerShell, local filesystem, Git installed
- Configuration:
```toml
[windows]
sandbox = "elevated"
```
- Date of reproduction: 2026-10-22

## Reproduction
1. Create an empty test directory on a local Windows drive and run `git init`.
2. Confirm that `Get-Location` and `git status --short` succeed in a regular PowerShell session.
3. Run Codex CLI 0.163.0 with the test repository as the current workspace and the `elevated` Windows sandbox.
4. Ask Codex to execute:
```powershell
Get-Location; git status --short; Test-Path .git
```

### Actual result
No shell command executes:
```text
Failed to create unified exec process: helper_unknown_error: setup refresh had errors
```

**Sanitized excerpts** from the sandbox setup log (paths and account identifiers removed):
```text
Windows sandbox selection: elevated
setup refresh: spawning <CODEX_INSTALL>/codex-windows-sandbox-setup.exe (cwd=<FRESH_GIT_WORKSPACE>)
read-acl-only mode: applying read ACLs
read ACL run completed
granting write ACE to <FRESH_GIT_WORKSPACE> for sandbox group and capability SID
write ACE grant failed on <FRESH_GIT_WORKSPACE>: open ACL target for update (READ_CONTROL | WRITE_DAC): Access is denied. (os error 5)
deny ACE failed on <FRESH_GIT_WORKSPACE>/.git: open deny ACL target for update (READ_CONTROL | WRITE_DAC): Access is denied. (os error 5)
setup error: setup refresh had errors
setup refresh: exited with status 1
```

The *separate, existing Git workspace* also failed, with:
```text
deny ACE failed on <EXISTING_GIT_WORKSPACE>/.git: open deny ACL target for update (READ_CONTROL | WRITE_DAC): Access is denied. (os error 5)
setup error: setup refresh had errors
```

### Expected result
Sandbox setup succeeds and permitted read-only commands run normally.

## Checks already performed
- Regular PowerShell: filesystem access, `git init`, and `git status --short` all work.
- On the existing `.git`: owner matches the Windows account, ACL inheritance is enabled, `icacls /verify` passes, and Administrators/SYSTEM have FullControl.
- A separate administrator PowerShell shows an elevated token; **the sandbox setup helper's effective token has not been verified**.
- No project ACL reset, ownership takeover, or Git metadata deletion was performed.
- Earlier, on 2026-10-12, switching to `sandbox = "unelevated"` allowed Codex to create and re-read a test file. That workaround has **not** been retested with CLI 0.163.0.

## Request
Could maintainers investigate why `codex-windows-sandbox-setup.exe` cannot acquire `WRITE_DAC` access in elevated sandbox mode even in a newly initialized workspace? Is there a supported non-destructive workaround or a fix release?

Related reports: #52862 and #53946. Unlike the existing-workspace-only reproduction described in #53946, the present case also reproduces in a newly initialized Git repository.

**Privacy note:** Raw logs are intentionally *not* attached because they contain Windows usernames and absolute local paths. The excerpts above are redacted; no account names, machine names, SIDs, tokens, or private repository contents are included.
